doc.title: Curtis Fuller — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Anticipation on the bandstand and a sideman's missed train
summary: Fuller explains why he covered parts the night before and how he handled the pianist who had a train to catch.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Now, you've got to restructure. It's like any business. He can't go downstairs and get a whole new cast of players, or workers, to run his club tonight. You know? There's going to be some snafus.
Something is going to go wrong or he is going to try to do everything, or whatever.

Yeah, like, you guys were together. You've got signs, feelings, you've done this enough together with the others. You’re anticipating, he's been around enough with you to know that he's going here now. You've got to do what I can do on the bandstand, I can’t slow down.
I saw you do it a couple times on the bandstand last night.
That’s pacing. That's knowing what you're going to do in the frame.

Well, it's more than that. Well, the last set, the reason I did it two or three times is because Sharpe had to catch a train and he had the ticket. He plays in the church choir, for the choir. He had to be there, he's a very diligent young man.
He went to church last night too, on the bandstand.

He went, will he stays in church. I fixed him. Since that guy didn't have a salary for him, I had to give him money so he could function and get home and get on the train and get to the thing that he loves a lot, playing for the church.
